video_title: AI, Infrastructure, and the Next Investment Cycle
gist: a16z growth team walks through its State of Markets slides: earnings-driven market gains, hyperscaler capex of $780B in 2026, shallow enterprise AI adoption (69% live vs 2% tracked), software bifurcation, and why top private companies stay private. Argues the cycle is early, not a bubble.

themes.theme: Tech as everything cycle and bubble debate

insights.claim: High-tech equipment, software and R&D account for roughly 55% of US capital spending, and tech is almost 40% of aggregate US stock market value, with eight of the top 10 valued companies being US tech firms.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Economy-wide capex and index concentration are now a single tech trade.

insights.claim: The AI buildout has just surpassed railroads as a percentage of GDP, and a16z's growth team expects cumulative figures to be roughly 20x higher in five to ten years.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Historical analogy used to argue the cycle is early, not late.

insights.claim: US stocks are up about 20% while market multiples are down about 20%, with the S&P 500 forward multiple below 20x, so the rally is earnings-driven rather than multiple expansion, unlike the dot-com era's ~100x PE leaders.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Core argument against the bubble thesis: earnings, not multiples, drive the market.

insights.claim: Since ChatGPT's launch almost four years ago the market is up 90% (17% annualized), yet it trades below 20x earnings growing ~15%, which differs from 2000 and 2021 when multiples and growth were decoupled.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: The instinct that 17% annualized must mean-revert ignores that earnings growth is matching it.

insights.claim: Cyclical memory companies are trading at roughly six to seven times forward earnings despite the AI demand surge.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Memory remains priced as a cyclical, a potential disconnect versus AI-demand narrative.

insights.claim: Capex of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle is about $780 billion in 2026, up from $416 billion in 2025, with expectations of over $1 trillion annually from 2027.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Capex nearly doubling year over year sets order-book demand for chips, power and construction.

insights.claim: Successive forecasts for the five largest hyperscalers' capex have repeatedly moved sharply higher, and spending once viewed as a ceiling has become near-term; the economy has underestimated the trend for four years.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Betting on capex plateau has been wrong repeatedly.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are investing essentially all of their near-term operating cash flow into the buildout, and demand outstrips supply in almost every case, with some data center supply chain items unobtainable until 2028.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Supply constraints extend through 2028, supporting suppliers' pricing power.

insights.claim: Agents running parallel and long-running tasks, including overnight, raise compute requirements far beyond the occasional-query model, making compute demand a 'model buster'.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Demand forecasts based on chat-query usage understate agent-driven compute.

insights.claim: OpenAI's massive compute commitments were criticized as reckless a year ago but are now seen as prescient, and OpenAI recently had to pause new subscriptions on its pro plans because of insatiable demand.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Capacity, not demand, is the binding constraint for leading labs.

insights.claim: Microsoft, Google and Amazon have about $1.7 trillion of combined cloud backlog, and consensus has hyperscaler free cash flow, depressed during the buildout, recovering from 2028 with substantial growth after.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Backlog gives a demand-side anchor for the FCF J-curve.

insights.claim: Amazon described a J-curve in which GPUs and TPUs have useful economic lives longer than expected, so shells and chips bought up front earn returns over a long period.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Depreciation-life assumptions underpin whether capex returns are adequate.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers that blinked and were less aggressive on capex and debt raising have regretted it, mirroring the model labs.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Market punishes under-investment more than debt-funded over-investment in this cycle.

insights.claim: Spot-market pricing for existing GPUs is attractive, signaling that any GPU brought online earns a strong return, with chip buyers paying much more than 12 to 24 months ago while still making high margins.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Rising GPU rental prices argue against a near-term glut.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capex should be viewed as someone else's order books, turning the tech boom into an industrial boom across chips, power and construction, and requiring financing, vendor management and capacity forecasting skills unlike traditional build-once software.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Investing in this supply chain requires different underwriting than software IP monetization.

themes.theme: Physical infrastructure and the age of atoms

insights.claim: Global infrastructure investment needs are estimated at $90 trillion through 2040, extending beyond AI and data centers to power, water, roads and transit.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: The investable infrastructure opportunity is broader than data centers.

insights.claim: a16z portfolio examples of the physical buildout include Anduril's massive manufacturing facility (87 football fields), Waymo's depot expansion, and SpaceX's $100 billion investment in Louisiana.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Winning founders increasingly execute factories as competitive advantage.

insights.claim: Founders from Tesla and SpaceX are prominent in a16z's portfolio because they learned that executing on the factory becomes a massive competitive advantage at scale.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Manufacturing-execution pedigree is a hiring and backing signal.

insights.claim: A recent US study found that for every 10% increase in data center capacity, residential electricity rates fell by 40 bps, because large stable customers spread the fixed costs of poles, wires and substations.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Counters the political narrative that data centers raise household power bills.

themes.theme: AI adoption depth and cost deflation

insights.claim: S&P 500 live AI deployments are at 69%, quantifiable impact is 30%, but metrics tracked over time are only 2%, showing adoption is shallow relative to headlines.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Large runway for deepening enterprise usage into recurring workflows.

insights.claim: Most enterprises still have AI exposure mostly through Microsoft Copilot, indicating how far they have to go.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Enterprise diffusion beyond Copilot and coding is the next leg.

insights.claim: Median AI vendor spending in the top 1% of companies is roughly eight times the level of the top 10% (Ramp-type spend data), showing power users pulling away.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: AI spend is highly concentrated among the most intensive adopters.

insights.claim: Within AI-native a16z portfolio companies, top users spend about $7,500 to $9,000 per month on AI versus a median of $200 to $400, over 20x.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Per-user AI spend has no near ceiling, expanding the revenue pool for token consumers.

insights.claim: AI tool spend relative to headcount cost is about 1% at forward-leaning Fortune 500 companies versus as high as 10% at the most AI-native portfolio companies.
insights.speaker: Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Gap shows how much diffusion remains if laggards converge.

insights.claim: Chime reports reducing cost to serve by over 10% a year for four years (nearly 50% compounded), supported by Decagon.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Hard public-company evidence of AI cost savings.

insights.claim: Shopify's AI Sidekick raised the share of merchants reaching five orders within 15 days of onboarding by 8%, a metric tied to retention.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: AI shows revenue-side impact via activation.

insights.claim: ServiceNow has reported more than $1 billion in AI ACV and a 9x increase in agentic deployments.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Incumbents are monetizing AI, not just startups.

insights.claim: Companies choosing to spend incremental AI dollars on efficiency rather than new revenue products reveal they see less opportunity; revenue upside is unbounded while cost savings are a latent, finite opportunity.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Use where CEOs direct AI dollars as a litmus test for opportunity.

insights.claim: Agent token usage on OpenRouter grew 14x, and caching has made Hebbia's financial chat workloads 10x cheaper to run.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Falling per-step costs make multi-step agents economical.

insights.claim: Databricks' smart router solves more problems at 35% lower cost than the strongest single model, and Elise AI's fine-tuned smaller model was 60% cheaper with much lower latency.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Routing and fine-tuning are margin levers for application companies.

insights.claim: Application companies should price on the customer's job done rather than model cost, so better routing lets them expand margins by not using the most expensive model for every step.
insights.speaker: Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Expect gross margin improvement at the best app companies.

insights.claim: A two-orders-of-magnitude cost drop (cited from newer labs) is a classic Jevons paradox that would unlock use cases currently prohibitively expensive.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Falling inference cost expands total demand rather than shrinking spend.

insights.claim: Revolut partnered with ElevenLabs, harnessing its voice model to securely connect with customer accounts, illustrating that the opportunity is harnessing model capabilities into reliable services.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Application-layer value lies in integrating models with company context.

insights.claim: Companies in the foundation model layer have together raised over $350 billion, and OpenAI and Anthropic's combined annualized revenue and net new revenue added exceed those of the best software companies ever built.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Lab revenue ramp is faster than any software precedent.

insights.claim: Only just over 2% of US households have a paying AI subscription, though AI subscriptions show some of the best retention ever seen in consumer, with smile-shaped curves.
insights.speaker: Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Low penetration with improving retention suggests long runway versus Amazon Prime (200M+ households) or Netflix (70M).

insights.claim: Josh Elman argues consumer AI is what people use daily, not what they expense, so 97% of households using AI without paying is unsurprising.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Subscription may not be the primary consumer monetization model.

insights.claim: Persistent proactive AI agents working in the background will not show up as screen time, making outside-in engagement data less useful for evaluating consumer AI.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Traditional engagement metrics (time spent) will mismeasure agent products.

insights.claim: Perplexity-type challengers and ChatGPT are taking more queries from traditional search, so consumer marketplaces must assess how much incremental demand agents can bring and how much profit comes from owning discovery.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Marketplaces face a strategic choice on agent access.

insights.claim: Amazon declined an agent integration while Instacart accepted; Amazon's advertising (over $70 billion) outpaces its operating profit ex-AWS, whereas Instacart has more online grocery penetration upside from incremental orders.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Players dependent on ad-funded discovery resist agents; those needing orders embrace them.

insights.claim: Google's search resilience came partly because high-monetizing queries like insurance and hotels required action AI could not yet take; if AI can act on users' behalf this changes.
insights.speaker: Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agentic action capability is the real risk to search ad pools.

insights.claim: The market reaction to the Amazon/agent news was net market cap positive across the ecosystem, with Meta's gains far exceeding marketplace losses.
insights.speaker: Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Markets see agents shifting profit pools rather than shrinking the total.

insights.claim: Lower-friction agent ordering could raise GMV and consumption, so profit pools may be reallocated while the overall economy gains, and the team expects meaningful macro productivity improvement within three years.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Positive-sum view; advertising pools could migrate to agent channels.

themes.theme: Public software, SaaS apocalypse and private markets

insights.claim: Roughly 75% of public software companies in the sample are profitable but only 30% grow 20% or more, and fewer than five grow above 30%, while nearly every private company a16z sees grows well above 30%.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Public software mix has shifted to slower-growth; growth is migrating to private AI-era companies.

insights.claim: IT budgets fund AI by cutting from or not adding to new SaaS projects, so incumbents must apply AI to existing distribution and show 98% gross dollar retention plus revenue growth acceleration to dispel SaaS-apocalypse fears.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Watch for revenue acceleration (target 10%+) at incumbents over 12 to 18 months.

insights.claim: The fear that everyone would vibe code their own software systems is clearly not what is happening in the market, with internal system-of-record rebuilds a poor use of engineering resources.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Build-vs-buy threat to SaaS has been overstated.

insights.claim: Cybersecurity, observability and vertical software have held up much better than horizontal applications, because AI-created agents and software generate new security and monitoring needs, as with CrowdStrike.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Screen software by how AI changes the customer's need for the product (Ali Ghodsi's 'chopping block').

insights.claim: The software index is back to where it began the year after an early-year SaaS apocalypse, but bifurcated into perceived AI winners and losers, with winners accelerating and capturing net new dollars.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Dispersion within software is the opportunity.

insights.claim: Stripe's SaaS customer data, which Stripe calls the 'renaissance', shows growth accelerating into 2026 across both young and mature businesses.
insights.speaker: Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Private operating data contradicts the narrative that SaaS is in decline.

insights.claim: Vertical AI companies such as Harvey, Abridge and EliseAI are growing faster than any precedents in their industries, which shows customers value orchestration and vertical workflows beyond the model.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Vertical AI remains a prime venture area.

insights.claim: The top six private companies by last round valuation (Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut) total about 2.4 trillion dollars, more than the combined market cap of IPOs in the last 10 years excluding SpaceX, and nearly the size of the Russell 2000.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Value creation is staying private longer; late-stage private is a major asset class.

insights.claim: a16z views the founder as the asset class and the IPO as just another financing event, with private status allowing longer-duration bets, while public listing can help trust, as Navan reaccelerated after going public.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Stay-private vs IPO is a founder-specific tradeoff.

insights.claim: Carta data show only 58% participation in tender offers, meaning employees choose not to sell because of conviction; a16z also favors frequent valuation resets for fresh M&A currency.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Employee holding behavior signals confidence; tenders compete with public RSUs.

insights.claim: Secondary-market discounts to last-round prices are now basically zero, versus meaningful discounts in 2021 to 2024.
insights.speaker: Alex Emerman
insights.so_what: Private valuations are viewed as fresh with net new buyers at the same price.

insights.claim: AI-related companies account for 86% of US VC deal activity in the 2026 snapshot, up from 65% in 2025.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Venture is now almost entirely an AI allocation.

insights.claim: a16z believes robotics could be larger than LLMs but probably 3 to 5 years earlier in its cycle, making it a massive investment area over the next five years.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Early positioning in robotics is a core growth-team priority.

insights.claim: Uber and Lyft represent about 1% of US miles traveled; with autonomous networks 14 times safer than humans, a16z expects this to expand at least an order of magnitude, and thinks the 17 million new US cars sold per year will all be autonomous within 10 years.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Autonomy could expand ride-hailing's share of miles dramatically.

insights.claim: American dynamism vendors such as Anduril, Saronic and Castelion are still less than 5% of military dollars spent, which a16z expects to grow dramatically.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Defense retooling remains early-stage share gain for new vendors.

insights.claim: Other areas a16z is excited about include long-running consumer agents, AI times bio for drug discovery, personal health advice, and enterprise diffusion beyond coding.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Signals a16z's growth-stage pipeline themes.
